Model Context Protocol (MCP): Enterprise Architecture, Protocol Internals & Production Python Implementation

A practical guide for architects and developers who want to understand MCP, build Python servers, and connect AI applications to enterprise services. It starts with the basic idea, then moves into protocol details, production design, and two complete examples.

MCP in plain language

MCP is a shared set of rules that lets an AI application connect to software tools and data. It gives the application a common way to ask, “What can this service do?” and then request one of those things.

A simple way to picture it: MCP is a common plug between an AI application and a service. The plug makes the connection predictable. It does not decide whether a user is allowed to take an action. The application and the service still need to apply their own safety, identity, and business rules.

PartPlain-language meaningExample
HostThe application that contains the AI model and the user interface. It chooses which MCP servers to connect to and what tools the model may see.An internal support assistant
ClientThe host’s MCP connection to one server. It sends and receives MCP messages.The support assistant’s connection to the order server
ServerA small service that offers a clear set of actions or information. It often calls an existing API or database behind the scenes.An order MCP server that calls the Orders API
ToolAn action the model may ask the host to run, such as looking up an order.get_order_status
ResourceNamed information the application can read and make available as context.A recent order history or service log
PromptA reusable set of instructions for a task. It helps people start a workflow in a consistent way.A customer-support triage template

A request, step by step

Suppose someone asks, “Has order ORD-1042 shipped?” Here is the path from the question to the answer:

  1. The host gives the model the relevant tool description, such as get_order_status, and its required input.
  2. The model decides that this tool can answer the question and asks the host to call it with {"order_id":"ORD-1042"}.
  3. The MCP client sends that request to the order server.
  4. The server checks the input and caller’s permissions, then calls the existing Orders API.
  5. The server returns a small result, for example {"status":"shipped","eta":"2026-10-17"}.
  6. The host gives the result back to the model, which explains it to the user.

The model does not reach into the database by itself. The host and server carry out the request, and the server must still enforce the same access rules as the existing system. For an action that changes data, such as changing a delivery address or issuing a refund, the application may also require a user confirmation.

What MCP does and does not do

MCP helps withMCP does not provide by itself
A common format for discovering tools and informationAn AI model, an agent, or a complete business workflow
Structured requests and responses between a host and a serverPermission to bypass the service’s authentication or authorization
Connecting an AI application to existing APIs and dataA replacement for REST, GraphQL, gRPC, databases, or message brokers
Optional updates and progress messages where the protocol supports themA guarantee that a model will choose the right tool or arguments

Keep this distinction: MCP standardizes how the request travels. Your application and backend still decide whether the request is allowed and what it means.

About this book

This guide shows how MCP can connect an AI application to systems your organization already runs. Your REST, GraphQL, gRPC, database, and Kafka systems stay in place. An MCP server exposes a small, useful set of actions or information from those systems in a format an AI host can understand.

The guide starts with the basic roles and messages, then moves through API design, Python implementation, security, gateways, and scaling. The diagrams show the main parts; the code shows how those parts fit together. Code examples were run with the versions described below. Sections that need Docker or a cluster say so.

Conventions

Python SDK. The examples target Python MCP SDK 2.x and were checked against version 2.3.0 with Python 3.12. The server name in 2.x is MCPServer; 1.x examples use FastMCP. If you install a newer SDK, check its migration notes before copying imports or transport code.

Two protocol versions appear in this guide. The legacy format starts with an initialize handshake and negotiates up to 2025-11-25. The modern format, 2026-07-28, has no initialize handshake or session ID; each request carries its own metadata. A client may call server/discover first to learn a server’s supported versions and capabilities. That call is optional in the protocol. The Python SDK’s high-level Client in automatic mode normally probes with it and can fall back to the legacy handshake for an older server. Check the version used by the actual connection rather than relying on a package constant.

Which examples use which format? Modules 1–7 and Capstone 1 intentionally show the legacy format. Capstone 2 uses the modern format for live subscriptions and a separate legacy connection for its sampling demonstration. The distinction matters because the modern format does not let a server send a separate request back to the host.

Features that changed. The 2026-07-28 specification deprecates roots, sampling, and MCP-level logging. Older integrations can still use some of these features over legacy connections, but new systems should not depend on them. Capstone 2 labels its legacy sampling example and explains the limit before the code.

Code that ran. Every Python file in this book was compiled and executed during writing. Tests used in-process harnesses and mocked HTTP — no live infrastructure was needed. Anything that genuinely needs Docker or a cluster carries this badge:

Run on a Docker-equipped machine — not verified in a sandbox.

Diagrams. All diagrams are hand-placed SVGs drawn for this book. They are simplifications: node counts are capped so the idea survives, and production systems will have more boxes. The text says what the diagram leaves out.

Python. All code is Python 3.12+ (X | Y unions, Annotated, async/await, contextlib.asynccontextmanager, Pydantic v2). Dependencies per module are listed in that module's pyproject.toml; capstones ship their own.

A note on explaining this aloud

This guide is meant to help you explain design choices in a review or interview. You do not need to memorize every message first. After each section, try to answer three questions: What problem does this solve? What can go wrong? What should the host or server do about it? Once you can explain the idea in ordinary words, the protocol details will be easier to remember.

Module 1 — MCP Protocol Internals & Wire-Level Mechanics

In plain language: MCP is a standard set of messages between an AI application and a service. This module explains the roles, the available actions and data, and how requests, replies, and updates travel.

Everything in MCP rides on a plain wire protocol. This module opens the hood: who the three actors are, the five primitives they exchange, the exact JSON-RPC bytes that cross the wire, and the two transports that carry them. Every claim here was verified by execution against mcp 2.3.0 (Python 3.12).

1.x → 2.x rename note. The MCP Python SDK renamed its flagship APIs in 2.x. The class the 1.x docs called FastMCP is now MCPServer, imported from mcp.server.mcpserver. The 1.x client factory streamablehttp_client is now streamable_http_client in mcp.client.streamable_http. The rest of this book uses the 2.x names throughout.

1.1 The tri-partite runtime: host, client, server

MCP splits one running system into three actors with sharply different jobs.

The MCP Host is the LLM application: the IDE, the desktop agent, the orchestrator process you build. It owns the model API key. It owns the user session. It decides which servers to connect and what the model is allowed to do with them.

The MCP Client is a protocol session manager. It speaks JSON-RPC to exactly one server, for one session. It runs the handshake. It negotiates capabilities. It dispatches tool calls and routes results back to the host. It holds no model and no domain logic. One client, one wire, one server.

The MCP Server is a domain capability adapter. It wraps a database, an API, a file tree, a payment gateway. It exposes that domain as tools, resources, and prompts. It never sees the user's LLM key. It never decides policy. It answers requests and emits notifications.

Why three, not two? Because the host wants many servers at once, and each server deserves its own room. One host spawns N isolated clients to talk to M domain servers simultaneously. Each client is a separate session with its own auth tokens, its own capability negotiation, its own failure domain. If the billing server crashes, the docs client's session keeps running. If a poisoned tool description slips into the orders server, it cannot leak into the billing session — there is no shared wire, no shared state, no shared client. Isolation is not a feature layered on top. It falls out of the topology: one client per server, per session.

In code terms: the host is your application process. The client is ClientSession from the mcp package, driven by your host code. The server is a separate process (or HTTP service) built with MCPServer. You will see all three ends running in the demos below.

1.2 The five primitives

Five primitives carry every interaction. Each one answers a different control question: who decides to invoke it.

Tools are model-controlled. The model sees a tool's name, description, and JSON Schema input contract. The model decides when to call it. Tools may have side effects: issuing refunds, creating tickets, running queries. That is the whole point — tools are how the model acts on the world. Because the model chooses arguments, the server validates every call against the schema before executing. In the demo below, calling issue_refund with a negative amount never reaches business logic: schema-level discipline starts at the signature.

Resources are application-controlled. The host application reads them, not the model on its own initiative. They are read-only data: file contents, audit logs, dashboard snapshots. Servers expose them behind custom URI schemes such as enterprise://orders/{id}/audit-log. A scheme names a domain; the path names a document. Resource templates cover families of resources — one handler answers every concrete URI that matches the template. Resources can also be subscriptions: the client calls subscribe_resource, and the server pushes notifications/resources/updated when the data changes. Read-only, addressable, subscribable — resources are the model's window into state it must not mutate.

Prompts are user-controlled. They are parameterized, versioned workflow templates the user (or the application on the user's behalf) selects. triage_ticket(ticket_id) does not do the triage. It returns the structured instructions that make triage repeatable. Prompts turn tribal knowledge into a named, reusable artifact.

Sampling inverts the usual direction. Normally the client calls the server. With sampling, the server sends sampling/createMessage and asks the host for an LLM completion. Why? Backend servers must never hold LLM API keys. Keys live with the host. When a tool needs reasoning — summarizing a document, drafting a reply — it asks the host to do it and gets the text back on the same wire. Agentic reasoning stays nested inside the host process. Version note: sampling was deprecated in the 2026-07-28 specification. It is still usable by older integrations on a legacy connection, but a modern connection has no server-to-host request channel for this call. Treat the example as a way to understand existing systems, not a recommendation for new ones.

Roots are host-defined boundaries. The host tells the server which filesystem paths or URI prefixes it may operate in, via list_roots_callback on the client side. The server asks roots/list and learns its sandbox. Roots keep a file-server tool from wandering outside the project directory. The host draws the fence; the server works inside it.

1.3 The JSON-RPC 2.0 wire lifecycle

MCP does not invent a transport protocol. It sends JSON-RPC 2.0 messages — requests with ids, responses, and id-less notifications — and gives each method a name like initialize or tools/call. The lifecycle has four phases. Every payload below is real, captured from a live stdio session (ref/wire.log), reproduced verbatim.

Phase 1 — Handshake: version and capability negotiation

The client opens with initialize. It states the newest protocol version it speaks and the capabilities it supports — here, roots change notifications and sampling:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": {"protocolVersion": "2026-07-28", "capabilities": {"roots": {"listChanged": true}, "sampling": {}}, "clientInfo": {"name": "wire-probe-client", "version": "0.1"}}}

The server answers with the highest version both sides speak, plus its own capability advertisement:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"capabilities":{"prompts":{"listChanged":false},"resources":{"listChanged":false,"subscribe":false},"tools":{"listChanged":false}},"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","serverInfo":{"name":"wire-probe","version":"1.0.0"}}}

Read that exchange closely. The client offered 2026-07-28 inside an initialize request — and the server answered 2025-11-25. That is not a failure. initialize is the legacy-era handshake: it negotiates the highest version both sides speak within the legacy wire, which tops out at 2025-11-25 in this SDK. The constant mcp.types.LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION reads "2026-07-28" because that is the modern wire format. It has no initialize handshake. The optional server/discover request tells a client which versions and capabilities a server supports; a client can also send a supported request directly and handle a version error. In the Python SDK, Client(mode="auto") normally sends a discovery probe first and falls back to the legacy handshake when needed. Modules 1–7 use legacy ClientSession examples. Capstone 2 uses the modern mcp.Client for subscriptions. Check the version of the connection you actually opened instead of assuming a constant describes every connection.

Then the client sends the session's first notification — no id, no response expected:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}

Phase 2 — Discovery: list everything before touching anything

A well-behaved client learns the server's surface before acting. Three list calls, three results:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list", "params": {}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"tools":[{"description":"Add two integers.","inputSchema":{"properties":{"a":{"title":"A","type":"integer"},"b":{"title":"B","type":"integer"}},"required":["a","b"],"type":"object","title":"addArguments"},"name":"add","outputSchema":{"properties":{"result":{"title":"Result","type":"integer"}},"required":["result"],"type":"object","title":"addOutput"}}]}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "resources/list", "params": {}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"resources":[{"description":"","mimeType":"text/plain","name":"hello","uri":"probe://hello"}]}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "prompts/list", "params": {}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"result":{"prompts":[{"arguments":[{"name":"name","required":true}],"description":"","name":"greet"}]}}

Notice tools/list returns the full JSON Schema for each tool's inputs and its outputSchema for structured results. The client can cache this and validate arguments before ever calling. Also notice what is not here: resource templates live under a separate method, resources/templates/list. resources/list only carries concrete, directly readable URIs.

Phase 3 — Execution: call, stream progress, cancel

The call carries its arguments plus _meta — the envelope for request-scoped metadata. Here the client attaches a progressToken so the server can stream progress against this exact request:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 40, "b": 2}, "_meta": {"progressToken": "tok-1"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"result":{"content":[{"text":"42","type":"text"}],"isError":false,"structuredContent":{"result":42}}}

Two result shapes in one payload: content for human-readable text, structuredContent for machine-consumable JSON. The model reads the text. Your application code reads the structure.

While the request runs, the server pushes progress notifications keyed by the token the client supplied:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/progress", "params": {"progressToken": "tok-1", "progress": 1, "total": 3, "message": "step 1 of 3"}}

Either side can abort a running request by naming its id:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/cancelled", "params": {"requestId": 5, "reason": "user interrupted"}}

Phase 4 — Errors: two channels, two meanings

MCP keeps two error channels apart, and confusing them breaks error handling. JSON-RPC errors mean the protocol machinery failed: the method does not exist, the params are malformed, the JSON does not parse. A call to a method the server never defined gets the standard code:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "bogus/method", "params": {}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"error":{"code":-32601,"message":"Method not found","data":"bogus/method"}}

The standard codes: -32700 parse error, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal error.

But an unknown tool name is not a protocol failure. The method tools/call exists; the tool does not. So the server returns a normal result with a self-healing payload:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 6, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "nope", "arguments": {}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"result":{"content":[{"text":"Unknown tool: nope","type":"text"}],"isError":true}}

This distinction is deliberate. A JSON-RPC error kills the request at the machinery level — the model sees an exception. An isError result hands the model a plain-language message it can recover from: re-read the tool list, fix the name, retry. Teach this hard. Retry loops and self-correction logic key off isError, not off exceptions.

The same lifecycle, one rung down: mcp.server.lowlevel.Server

MCPServer is sugar over mcp.server.lowlevel.Server. The low-level class takes explicit request handlers — no decorators, no schema derivation. This is the complete, runnable version (executed green over real stdio):

"""Module 1 demo (c): the SAME lifecycle with mcp.server.lowlevel.Server —
no MCPServer sugar. You build the JSON-RPC handlers by hand.

This is what MCPServer does for you: it converts decorated Python functions
into ServerCapabilities, ListToolsResult, CallToolResult, etc.

Run:  ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/.venv/bin/python demo_lowlevel.py
"""

import asyncio
import sys

import mcp.types as types
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.stdio import StdioServerParameters, stdio_client
from mcp.server.lowlevel import NotificationOptions, Server
from mcp.server.stdio import stdio_server


# ---- Hand-built handlers -----------------------------------------------------
# Low-level handlers receive (context, params) and return SDK result types.
# Every method name on the wire is a literal string you control here.

async def handle_list_tools(ctx, params: types.PaginatedRequestParams) -> types.ListToolsResult:
    return types.ListToolsResult(
        tools=[
            types.Tool(
                name="add",
                description="Add two integers.",
                inputSchema={
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}},
                    "required": ["a", "b"],
                },
            )
        ]
    )


async def handle_call_tool(ctx, params: types.CallToolRequestParams) -> types.CallToolResult:
    if params.name != "add":
        # Note: unknown tool = isError payload, NOT a JSON-RPC error (-32601).
        return types.CallToolResult(
            content=[types.TextContent(type="text", text=f"Unknown tool: {params.name}")],
            isError=True,
        )
    total = params.arguments["a"] + params.arguments["b"]
    return types.CallToolResult(
        content=[types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(total))],
        structuredContent={"result": total},
        isError=False,
    )


app = Server(
    "wire-probe-lowlevel",
    version="1.0.0",
    on_list_tools=handle_list_tools,
    on_call_tool=handle_call_tool,
)


async def run_server() -> None:
    async with stdio_server() as (read_stream, write_stream):
        await app.run(
            read_stream,
            write_stream,
            app.create_initialization_options(NotificationOptions()),
        )


# ---- Client -------------------------------------------------------------------
async def run_client() -> None:
    params = StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable, args=[__file__, "--server"])
    async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            init = await session.initialize()
            print("negotiated protocolVersion:", init.protocol_version)
            assert init.protocol_version == "2025-11-25"
            assert init.server_info.name == "wire-probe-lowlevel"

            tools = await session.list_tools()
            assert [t.name for t in tools.tools] == ["add"]
            print("inputSchema:", tools.tools[0].input_schema)

            result = await session.call_tool("add", {"a": 40, "b": 2})
            assert result.is_error is False
            assert result.structured_content == {"result": 42}
            print("structured content:", result.structured_content)

            bad = await session.call_tool("nope", {})
            assert bad.is_error is True
            print("unknown tool payload:", bad.content[0].text)

            print("LOWLEVEL ROUND-TRIP PASSED")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--server" in sys.argv:
        asyncio.run(run_server())
    else:
        asyncio.run(run_client())

Run it with ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/.venv/bin/python demo_lowlevel.py. Expected output: negotiated 2025-11-25, the add input schema, structured content {"result": 42}, the unknown-tool payload, and LOWLEVEL ROUND-TRIP PASSED.

And the full MCPServer version with one tool, one resource template, and one prompt — exercised over the same real stdio wire (also executed green):

"""Module 1 demo (a): one MCPServer with a tool, a resource and a prompt,
exercised over a REAL stdio session (newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout).

Run the round-trip assertions with:
    ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/.venv/bin/python demo_stdio.py

The script spawns ITSELF as the server subprocess (via stdio_client) so a single
file shows both ends of the wire.
"""

import asyncio
import sys

from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.stdio import StdioServerParameters, stdio_client
from mcp.server.mcpserver import Context, MCPServer

# ---- Server definition ------------------------------------------------------
# MCPServer is the 2.x name (1.x called it FastMCP). It builds on
# mcp.server.lowlevel.Server and turns Python signatures into JSON Schema.

server = MCPServer("demo-billing", version="1.0.0")


@server.tool()
def issue_refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> dict:
    """Issue a refund for an order. Side effect: model-controlled action.

    The JSON Schema for input validation is derived from this signature:
    order_id: string (required), amount: number (required).
    """
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
    return {"order_id": order_id, "refunded": amount, "status": "processed"}


@server.resource("enterprise://orders/{order_id}/audit-log")
def audit_log(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Read-only domain data behind a custom URI scheme.

    Resource *templates* let the client address many resources through one
    handler. Application-controlled: the host decides when to read it.
    """
    return f"audit-log for {order_id}\n- 09:00 charge $42.00\n- 10:15 refund issued"


@server.prompt()
def triage_ticket(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Parameterized, versioned workflow template. User-controlled."""
    return (
        f"Triage support ticket {ticket_id}:\n"
        "1. Read the ticket summary.\n"
        "2. Classify as billing/technical/account.\n"
        "3. Suggest the next action in one sentence."
    )


@server.tool()
async def slow_report(steps: int, ctx: Context) -> dict:
    """Demonstrates progress: the server reports _meta-driven notifications."""
    for i in range(steps):
        await ctx.report_progress(i + 1, steps, f"step {i + 1} of {steps}")
    return {"steps": steps, "done": True}


async def run_server() -> None:
    # stdio transport: one JSON-RPC message per newline on stdin/stdout.
    # run_stdio_async is the awaitable form; .run() would call anyio.run() itself.
    await server.run_stdio_async()


# ---- Client: drives the full lifecycle over the real wire --------------------
async def run_client() -> None:
    params = StdioServerParameters(
        command=sys.executable,
        args=[__file__, "--server"],
    )
    seen_progress: list[dict] = []

    async def on_progress(progress: float, total: float | None, message: str | None) -> None:
        seen_progress.append({"progress": progress, "total": total, "message": message})

    async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            # Phase 1: initialize -> notifications/initialized. initialize() sends
            # the request, then the SDK fires notifications/initialized itself.
            init = await session.initialize()
            print("negotiated protocolVersion:", init.protocol_version)
            assert init.protocol_version == "2025-11-25"

            # Phase 2: discovery.
            tools = await session.list_tools()
            names = [t.name for t in tools.tools]
            print("tools:", names)
            assert names == ["issue_refund", "slow_report"]

            resources = await session.list_resources()
            print("resources:", [(r.name, r.uri) for r in resources.resources])

            templates = await session.list_resource_templates()
            tmpl_uris = [t.uri_template for t in templates.resource_templates]
            print("resource templates:", tmpl_uris)
            assert any("audit-log" in u for u in tmpl_uris)

            prompts = await session.list_prompts()
            print("prompts:", [p.name for p in prompts.prompts])
            assert [p.name for p in prompts.prompts] == ["triage_ticket"]

            # Phase 3: execution.
            result = await session.call_tool(
                "issue_refund", {"order_id": "o-42", "amount": 42.0}
            )
            print("call result:", result.content[0].text)
            assert result.is_error is False
            assert "o-42" in result.content[0].text or result.structured_content

            # Unknown tool -> NOT a JSON-RPC error; a self-healing payload.
            bad = await session.call_tool("nope", {})
            assert bad.is_error is True
            print("unknown tool payload:", bad.content[0].text)

            # Progress streaming: the client registered a progress callback and the
            # server emitted notifications/progress because the params carried _meta.
            await session.call_tool("slow_report", {"steps": 3}, progress_callback=on_progress)
            assert len(seen_progress) == 3, seen_progress
            print("progress notifications:", seen_progress)

            # Resources and prompts round-trip.
            page = await session.read_resource("enterprise://orders/o-42/audit-log")
            assert "o-42" in page.contents[0].text
            print("resource text:", page.contents[0].text.splitlines()[0])

            prompt = await session.get_prompt("triage_ticket", {"ticket_id": "T-7"})
            assert "T-7" in prompt.messages[0].content.text
            print("prompt text:", prompt.messages[0].content.text.splitlines()[0])

            print("ALL ROUND-TRIP ASSERTIONS PASSED")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--server" in sys.argv:
        asyncio.run(run_server())
    else:
        asyncio.run(run_client())

Sampling demo: the server asks, the host answers

This is the complete runnable demo (executed green). The tool calls ctx.session.create_message, which goes out as a server-to-client sampling/createMessage request on the existing session. The client's sampling_callback answers — here a mock LLM so the test runs offline. In production, that callback calls the provider with the host's API key:

"""Module 1 demo (b): sampling — the server asks the HOST for a completion.

The server holds no LLM API key. It sends `sampling/createMessage`; the client
(host-side callback) answers. The backend stays a dumb domain adapter while
agentic reasoning stays nested inside the host process.

Run:  ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/.venv/bin/python demo_sampling.py
"""

import asyncio
import sys

import mcp.types as types
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.stdio import StdioServerParameters, stdio_client
from mcp.server.mcpserver import Context, MCPServer

server = MCPServer("demo-sampling", version="1.0.0")


@server.tool()
async def summarize(text: str, ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Ask the host LLM to summarize. The server never touches an LLM API key.

    create_message goes out on the EXISTING session wire as a server->client
    request (method `sampling/createMessage`). The reply flows back as the
    JSON-RPC response. Reasoning stays nested: server -> host -> LLM.

    Ground-truth note: mcp 2.3.0 prints an MCPDeprecationWarning that sampling
    is deprecated as of the 2026-07-28 modern era (SEP-2577). The legacy wire
    taught in this module — the handshake negotiates 2025-11-25 — still treats
    sampling/createMessage as current. The warning documents where the spec is
    heading.
    """
    result = await ctx.session.create_message(
        messages=[
            types.SamplingMessage(
                role="user",
                content=types.TextContent(type="text", text=f"Summarize: {text}"),
            )
        ],
        max_tokens=50,
    )
    return f"host LLM said: {result.content.text}"


async def run_server() -> None:
    await server.run_stdio_async()


# ---- Client (host) side ------------------------------------------------------
# The host owns the model. It answers sampling/createMessage through this
# callback. In production this calls the LLM provider; here it is a mock so
# the test runs offline and green.
async def mock_llm(
    context: object, params: types.CreateMessageRequestParams
) -> types.CreateMessageResult:
    user_text = params.messages[0].content.text
    return types.CreateMessageResult(
        role="assistant",
        content=types.TextContent(type="text", text=f"MOCK-SUMMARY of {user_text!r}"),
        model="mock-llm-1",
        stop_reason="endTurn",
    )


async def run_client() -> None:
    params = StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable, args=[__file__, "--server"])
    async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(
            read,
            write,
            sampling_callback=mock_llm,
            sampling_capabilities=types.SamplingCapability(),
        ) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            result = await session.call_tool("summarize", {"text": "refund policy v3"})
            print("tool result:", result.content[0].text)
            assert "MOCK-SUMMARY" in result.content[0].text
            print("SAMPLING ROUND-TRIP PASSED: server -> client -> (mock LLM) -> server")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--server" in sys.argv:
        asyncio.run(run_server())
    else:
        asyncio.run(run_client())

Note what the client had to declare: it passes sampling_callback and advertises sampling_capabilities in its initialize (the captured wire-probe-client did exactly this with "capabilities": {"sampling": {}}). The server checks that capability before asking — a server that requests sampling from a client that did not advertise it gets refused. Consent to be asked is negotiated up front, in Phase 1.

1.4 Transports: how the bytes travel

The wire protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0. The transport decides how those messages move between processes and machines. MCP has three, of which two matter today.

stdio: spawn and talk over pipes

The host starts the server as a child process. The client writes JSON-RPC messages to the child's stdin and reads responses from its stdout — newline-delimited JSON, one message per line. No HTTP stack, no ports, no TLS. Startup is one subprocess call.

That simplicity is also the ceiling. Pipes cannot cross machines. The server must run on the same box as the host. So stdio serves local desktop and IDE agents: Claude Desktop, VS Code extensions, your own CLI agent spawning a billing adapter next to it. Auth is usually ambient — if you can spawn the process, you are trusted. For anything remote, stdio is the wrong tool.

Legacy HTTP+SSE: the awkward middle

Before Streamable HTTP, MCP's remote transport split traffic across two endpoints: a POST endpoint carried client-to-server messages, and a long-lived GET stream using Server-Sent Events carried server-to-client push. Two endpoints meant two connection setups, two things to route through load balancers and proxies, and session state pinned across both. It worked, but every deployment detail was doubled. The spec replaced it.

Streamable HTTP: one endpoint, session header, SSE upgrade

Modern MCP collapses remote traffic onto a single POST endpoint — /mcp by convention. The client posts JSON-RPC there. The server answers with an Mcp-Session-Id response header, and the client sends that header on every subsequent request to stay in the same session. When the server needs to push — progress notifications, notifications/resources/updated, sampling requests — the POST response upgrades to an SSE stream on the same endpoint. One URL, one session token, bidirectional when needed.

The SDK exposes this as a Starlette app:

app = server.streamable_http_app(
    stateless_http=False,      # keep sessions server-side (default)
    session_idle_timeout=1800, # evict idle sessions after 30 min
    max_sessions=10000,        # backpressure on session count
)
server.run(transport="streamable-http")   # or "stdio" | "sse"

And the client side, in 2.x naming:

import httpx2  # the SDK's HTTP layer; pass an httpx2 client, not httpx
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamable_http_client  # 2.x; 1.x: streamablehttp_client
from mcp import ClientSession

async with streamable_http_client(
    "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
    http_client=httpx2.AsyncClient(headers={"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}),
) as (read, write):
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()
        tools = await session.list_tools()

Note the injected httpx.AsyncClient: this is where enterprise auth rides. Bearer tokens, mTLS client certs, custom headers — they attach to the HTTP layer, not the protocol. The protocol never sees your credentials. That separation is why one host can hold N clients with N different auth postures, one per session, exactly as section 1.1 drew it.

stateless_http=True: what you gain, what you lose

streamable_http_app(stateless_http=True) drops server-side sessions. Every request stands alone. You gain painless horizontal scale-out: any replica can answer any request, no sticky sessions, no session-store replication. You lose everything that needs the server to remember the client or reach it unprompted: server-to-client push, sampling/createMessage (server-initiated requests need a session to travel on), and resource subscriptions. Stateless mode suits request/response tool APIs behind a load balancer. Stateful mode suits long-lived agent sessions with progress, push, and nested reasoning. Pick by asking one question: does the server ever need to speak first? If yes, stay stateful.

What you can now explain aloud

  • Why MCP has three actors, and why one host runs N clients for M servers.
  • The five primitives, each named by who controls it.
  • The four wire phases, with real payloads: initialize negotiation, discovery, call with _meta progress, and the two error channels.
  • Why an unknown tool returns isError while an unknown method returns -32601.
  • How sampling keeps LLM keys on the host.
  • When stdio fits, why HTTP+SSE died, and what stateless Streamable HTTP trades away.

Module 2 puts these mechanics under enterprise load: auth at the transport edge, multi-tenancy across sessions, and the failure modes this chapter's isolation story was built to contain.

Module 2 — MCP vs REST & Microservice APIs: The Architectural Shift

In plain language: REST APIs give software fixed endpoints to call. MCP gives an AI host a standard way to find and request selected operations. The API stays behind the MCP server; MCP does not replace it.

Every API style encodes an assumption about its caller. REST assumes the caller is deterministic: code a human wrote, a compiler checked, and a deploy froze before the first request ever fired. gRPC assumes the same, with stronger typing. The entire apparatus — OpenAPI specs, generated clients, status-code taxonomies, versioned URLs — exists to serve a caller whose behavior is fixed at design time.

An LLM agent breaks that assumption. It decides what to call, with what arguments, in what order, while it is running. Its call sequence is an emergent product of its reasoning, not a path a developer traced in advance. Handing such a caller a contract written for a compiler is like handing a tourist a subway map in a language they cannot read. All the information is there. None of it is usable under time pressure.

This module is about the shift that follows. Not a new transport. Not a replacement for REST. A new layer, with a new audience: contracts written for readers instead of compilers.

2.1 The caller changed first

Start with the concrete difference, because everything else derives from it.

A traditional service client is a function. Given an input, it walks a path its author drew: validate, call, branch on the status code, return. If the API grows a new error shape, the client does not adapt. It crashes, or swallows, until a human ships a new version. The client is closed at build time.

An agent is a loop. It reads the user's goal, reads the available tools, picks one, reads the result, and decides the next step. Nothing about the sequence is fixed before the first turn. If a tool returns a failure the agent has never seen, the agent does what a developer would do in the next sprint: read the message, adjust, retry. The loop is open at runtime.

Once you see the caller as a loop, the old contract's virtues become vices. Terse payloads save bandwidth but cost comprehension. Status codes are precise but demand pre-written branches. Design-time discovery is efficient but freezes capability. Each of these was the right trade when the reader was a compiler. Each is the wrong trade when the reader is a model.

MCP is the protocol that re-trades them.

2.2 The comparison matrix

The table states the differences. The paragraphs after it explain why each difference exists. Read the why; the table alone is just vocabulary.

Dimension REST / gRPC MCP The shift in one line
Primary consumer Deterministic code, written and compiled at design time A non-deterministic LLM reasoning loop, deciding at runtime The contract's reader changed from compiler to model
Discovery Design time: OpenAPI / Proto files, generated clients Runtime: tools/list returns schemas plus prose descriptions, every session Capabilities are introduced per session, not installed
Granularity Fine-grained CRUD resources, one endpoint per state transition Coarse-grained business intents, one tool per workflow Turn economics: one decision per business action
Statefulness Stateless request/response Stateful negotiated sessions: initialize, roots, subscriptions, progress, cancellation The caller persists across turns, so the protocol does too
Error recovery Typed status codes; the caller branches at design time isError: true plus natural-language remediation; the agent self-corrects on the next turn Errors are addressed to a reader that can change its mind
Versioning URL / media-type versions (/v1, /v2); a new address per breaking change protocolVersion negotiation; additive evolution; deprecations described in prose The model re-reads the contract every session
Auth model The client is a known principal; per-request tokens and scopes The host holds user authN and model keys; the server transports identity; authZ stays in the domain service The agent is a delegate, not a principal
Payload shape Terse, machine-shaped, bandwidth-frugal Verbose and self-describing; content for the model plus structuredContent for code Comprehension, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck
Latency profile Milliseconds, p99-bounded, cached aggressively Seconds to minutes per turn; generous timeouts; cancellation is first-class Budget per task, not per request
Testability Deterministic contract tests: request X yields byte-identical Y Deterministic tool-contract tests plus statistical evals of the loop Assert what the server guarantees; measure the caller

2.2.1 Primary consumer

REST and gRPC were built for callers whose shape is known when the client is written. A developer reads the docs once, the generator emits a client, and the machine never reads the docs at all. Terseness is affordable because the only reader that matters read everything up front.

MCP was built for a caller that reads the contract on every turn, inside its context window, while deciding what to do next. The model's "compilation step" happens at runtime, in prose. A contract that is merely parseable is not enough; it must be legible to something that reasons in language. That is the root difference, and every row below is a branch of it.

2.2.2 Discovery

REST discovery happens before runtime. You read the spec, generate the client, pin the version, and ship. The client never asks the server what it can do, because a human already told it.

MCP discovery happens during runtime. The client calls tools/list and gets back JSON Schemas paired with human-readable descriptions, fresh, every session. This exists because an agent cannot be recompiled when the API changes. Its capabilities are not installed; they are introduced, each session, in language.

That is also why the tool description is a first-class protocol field rather than documentation garnish. In REST, docs are for the developer and the machine ignores them. In MCP, the description is load-bearing: it is the text the caller actually reads before choosing. A vague description is not a docs problem here. It is a routing bug.

2.2.3 Granularity

REST resources are fine-grained: one endpoint per noun, one verb per state transition. Fetch the order, check its status, post the refund, poll the refund. Each call is cheap and precise, which is exactly right when the caller is code that chains them for free.

MCP tools are coarse-grained business intents: issue_refund(order_id, amount) does the whole job behind one name. The reason is turn economics. Every tool call costs the agent a reasoning turn, tokens in and out, and seconds of latency. A five-call CRUD choreography is five chances to pick the wrong next step, five round trips, and five turns of context burned. Coarse intents push the choreography down into deterministic code, where sequencing is cheap and safe, and leave the model one decision per business action.

The trade is real. Someone must now design verbs a model can choose between, and "chose the wrong verb" becomes a failure mode CRUD never had. Granularity moved the complexity; it did not delete it.

2.2.4 Statefulness

REST is stateless by doctrine. Each request carries its credentials and its context, which is why REST scales horizontally without thought.

MCP is stateful by negotiation. The session opens with an initialize handshake, both sides agree on a protocolVersion, and the connection then carries roots (client-side context the server may read), subscriptions, progress notifications, and cancellation. The state exists because an agent's task spans many turns, and re-sending the world on every call would drown the model's context window. Progress and cancellation exist because a reasoning loop can run for minutes, and "stop this runaway turn" has to be a protocol primitive rather than a socket timeout.

The price is everything REST gave up on purpose: session affinity, idle timeouts, session caps. The SDK is honest about the cost — streamable_http_app takes session_idle_timeout and max_sessions, and it ships a stateless_http=True escape hatch for call patterns that genuinely are one-shot. Stateful is the default because agentic work usually is not.

2.2.5 Error recovery

The short version, with the full treatment in §2.3: REST errors are addressed to code, MCP errors to a reader that can change its mind. Status codes assume the recovery branch was written before the failure ever happened. isError plus remediation text assumes the recovery will be invented after the failure, on the next turn.

2.2.6 Versioning

REST versions with addresses. /v1/ becomes /v2/ because old clients are frozen binaries that cannot learn new shapes, so breaking changes need new URLs and the old ones live on until the last client migrates.

In the legacy format, initialize carries protocolVersion; client and server agree on the highest legacy version they both support. The examples here use 2025-11-25. The modern format is 2026-07-28. It has no initialize handshake; server/discover is an optional way for a client to learn the server’s supported versions and capabilities. Modern clients use subscriptions/listen for live updates. Check the version of the connection you actually opened instead of assuming a package constant describes it.

Tools themselves evolve additively: new tools, new optional fields. The model re-reads tools/list every session, so a deprecation can be described ("prefer issue_refund_v2; issue_refund is legacy") instead of versioned away. But MCP has a breaking change REST never had: semantic drift. Rename a tool and every model that learned the old name from training data keeps calling the ghost. In REST you break clients you can count. In MCP you break callers you cannot see.

2.2.7 Auth model

In REST, the client is a known principal. It presents a bearer token or a client certificate, scopes are checked per request, and the identity is stable across calls.

The model is not the user’s identity. The host signs the user in and keeps the credentials needed to connect. When the host calls an MCP server, the server must know which user or service is making the request. It can pass that identity to the existing backend, which checks whether the caller may take the action — for example, issue this refund. MCP does not grant permission by itself. Older examples use sampling to ask the host for a model response; that feature is deprecated, so new systems should keep model calls in the host.

The split exists for leverage. If every tool re-implements authZ, you get N inconsistent permission models and the classic backend-for-frontend trap, one copy per surface. The MCP layer transports identity. It does not adjudicate it.

2.2.8 Payload shape

REST payloads are terse and machine-shaped: short keys, bare ids, paginated lists. Bandwidth was the constraint when the style was born, and machines do not need adjectives.

MCP payloads are verbose and self-describing: full field names, prose descriptions, and the CallToolResult habit of returning both content (text the model reads) and structuredContent (data downstream code parses). The redundancy is the point. Bandwidth is cheap now; model comprehension is the bottleneck. A model handed {"o":"ORD-004213","a":42.0} must guess what o means, and guessing is where agents go wrong. A model handed {"order_id":"ORD-004213","amount":42.0} plus a one-line description needs no guess. Everything a compiler would strip as waste is load-bearing for a reader.

2.2.9 Latency profile

REST chases milliseconds: p99 budgets, aggressive caching, connection reuse. MCP lives in seconds to minutes per turn, because each tool call sits inside a reasoning loop that may chain five or twenty calls before answering.

This inverts the optimization target. Shaving 5 ms off a tool is pointless if the agent needs five turns to do the job. One coarse intent that finishes in a single 800 ms call beats five 40 ms CRUD calls wrapped in four extra reasoning turns. Timeouts must be generous — the client SDK's read_timeout_seconds exists for exactly this — and cancellation is a first-class notification, because a stuck tool holds a reasoning loop hostage, not just a socket. You stop budgeting latency per request and start budgeting it per task.

2.2.10 Testability

REST is tested deterministically: given request X, expect byte-identical response Y. Contract tests, property tests, replayed traffic.

MCP splits the pyramid. The tool's contract is still tested deterministically — schemas, error shapes, invariants, the exact remediation strings — because the server side is still code. But the caller's behavior can only be evaluated statistically: did the agent pick the right tool, did it recover from isError, did it stop after success? You cannot assert what a non-deterministic caller will do. You can only assert what the server guarantees, then measure the loop against an eval harness. Teams that try to unit-test the agent's choices end up testing the model's mood. Teams that unit-test the tool contract and eval the loop get signal.

2.3 The self-healing feedback loop

This is the row that deserves its own section, because it is the mechanism people feel first when they move from APIs to agents.

Why HTTP 422 breaks traditional code

In a traditional integration, the caller enumerates failure modes at design time:

resp = client.post("/refunds", params={"order_id": order_id, "amount": amount})
if resp.status_code == 422:
    ...  # someone wrote this branch six months ago, for a shape they imagined
elif resp.status_code == 409:
    ...

The error body is typed for machines:

{"detail": [{"loc": ["query", "order_id"], "msg": "string does not match regex",
             "type": "string_pattern_mismatch", "input": "o-99"}]}

This works while the set of failures is closed and known. It breaks the moment a failure arrives that nobody branched on: an unseen validation shape, a new error code from a downstream deploy, a field renamed by another team. The caller then has three options, all bad: crash, swallow, or misinterpret. Production systems mostly do the second and third, which is why "the API returned 200 but the data is wrong" is a whole genre of outage.

The deeper issue is structural. The contract describes success completely and failure approximately. Recovery logic is written by a human, once, before the failure exists. An unseen validation shape is not a handled case; it is a crash wearing a JSON costume.

Why isError heals

A CallToolResult with isError: true does not ask the caller to have predicted the failure. It hands the failure, in prose, to a caller whose entire job is revising its plan:

{"content": [{"type": "text",
              "text": "order_id must match ORD-[0-9]{6}; you sent 'o-99'. Retry with a six-digit order id such as 'ORD-004213'."}],
 "isError": true}

Compare the two payloads. "string_pattern_mismatch" names the failure category. The remediation names the category, shows the violation, states the rule, and gives an example. The model does on turn N+1 what a developer would do in the next sprint: read the message, fix the argument, retry. No branch was written. No deploy happened.

The agent's next turn, narrated

Turn 1. The agent is refunding a customer. It copies an order id from the ticket text and calls issue_refund with order_id="o-99". The ticket's author abbreviated; the agent did not know.

Observation. The tool returns isError: true with the remediation above. The result is not an exception. The loop does not break. The failure arrives as content, the same channel as every other observation.

Turn 2. The model's reasoning, in plain terms: the tool expects ORD- followed by six digits; o-99 has the wrong prefix and the wrong length; the ticket subject line mentions order ORD-004213. It retries with order_id="ORD-004213". The tool returns the refund receipt. The task completes.

None of this is magic, and none of it is guaranteed. It is engineered. A vague error — "invalid input" — does not heal, because the model cannot invent the pattern from nothing. Self-healing rests on a contract every tool author must honor: each error message states (1) what was wrong, (2) the expected shape, and (3) a concrete example. Miss any of the three and the loop degrades to guessing.

A deliberate asymmetry on the wire

Two facts from the protocol's wire behavior belong here, because they show the philosophy is not an accident.

An unknown tool name does not raise a JSON-RPC error. The server returns a normal CallToolResult with "isError": true and a plain-language message ("Unknown tool: nope"). The loop survives the typo and reads the correction.

An unknown method does raise one: {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}. The peers disagree about the protocol itself, and there is nothing for the reader to heal — fail fast.

Tool-level mistakes are recoverable by the reader. Protocol-level mistakes are not. The protocol refuses to crash the loop for the first kind and refuses to negotiate the second.

Demo: the same failure, both philosophies

One runnable script. The FastAPI endpoint returns 422 for the bad id; the MCP tool returns an isError result with remediation text for the same input. The script asserts both, then plays the agent's next turn — retry with the corrected id — and asserts success. No network, no Docker.

"""Module 2 demo — the same validation failure, two error philosophies.

Side A (REST): a FastAPI endpoint rejects a bad order_id with HTTP 422.
Side B (MCP):  an MCP tool rejects the same input with a CallToolResult whose
               isError flag is true and whose text tells the caller exactly
               how to fix the argument.

The script asserts both behaviors, then plays the agent's next turn: read the
remediation text, correct the argument, retry, and succeed.

Run (no network, no Docker):
    ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/.venv/bin/python \
        ~/workspace/build/mcp-guide/code/module-02/demo_self_healing.py
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import re

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

import mcp.types as types
from mcp.server.lowlevel import Server

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Shared domain rule. In production this validation lives in the microservice;
# both the REST endpoint and the MCP tool enforce it. The demo's point is not
# the validation logic — it is how the *failure* is reported and who is
# expected to recover from it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ORDER_ID_RE = re.compile(r"ORD-[0-9]{6}")

REMEDIATION_TEMPLATE = (
    "order_id must match ORD-[0-9]{{6}}; you sent '{value}'. "
    "Retry with a six-digit order id such as 'ORD-004213'."
)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Side A — REST: the deterministic microservice endpoint.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rest_app = FastAPI(title="billing-rest")


@rest_app.post("/refunds")
def create_refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> dict:
    """Issue a refund. Caller is deterministic code, contract fixed at design time."""
    if not ORDER_ID_RE.fullmatch(order_id):
        # Typed status code + machine-shaped body. Recovery was supposed to be
        # branched on at design time, when this endpoint was integrated.
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=422,
            detail=[{
                "loc": ["query", "order_id"],
                "msg": "string does not match regex",
                "type": "string_pattern_mismatch",
                "input": order_id,
            }],
        )
    return {"refund_id": "RF-004213", "order_id": order_id, "amount": amount}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Side B — MCP: the agentic presentation layer over the same domain rule.
# Registered as the low-level server's tools/call handler, so the object
# returned is the exact CallToolResult the protocol puts on the wire
# (note the "isError": true spelling in the JSON below).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
async def handle_call_tool(
    ctx: object, params: types.CallToolRequestParams
) -> types.CallToolResult:
    order_id = params.arguments.get("order_id", "")
    if params.name != "issue_refund":
        # Wire fact: an unknown tool name is NOT a protocol error. The server
        # returns a normal result with isError set, so the agent's reasoning
        # loop survives the typo and can read the correction.
        return types.CallToolResult(
            is_error=True,
            content=[types.TextContent(
                type="text",
                text=f"Unknown tool: {params.name}. Available tools: issue_refund.",
            )],
        )
    if not ORDER_ID_RE.fullmatch(order_id):
        # Self-healing contract: every error message states (1) what was wrong,
        # (2) the expected shape, (3) a concrete example. That triple is what
        # lets the model repair its own arguments on the next turn.
        return types.CallToolResult(
            is_error=True,
            content=[types.TextContent(
                type="text",
                text=REMEDIATION_TEMPLATE.format(value=order_id),
            )],
        )
    return types.CallToolResult(
        content=[types.TextContent(type="text", text="Refund issued.")],
        structured_content={
            "refund_id": "RF-004213",
            "order_id": order_id,
            "amount": params.arguments.get("amount"),
        },
    )


mcp_server = Server("billing-mcp", on_call_tool=handle_call_tool)


async def call_issue_refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> types.CallToolResult:
    """Drive the registered handler in-process, exactly as tools/call would."""
    params = types.CallToolRequestParams(
        name="issue_refund",
        arguments={"order_id": order_id, "amount": amount},
    )
    return await handle_call_tool(None, params)


def demo_rest() -> None:
    client = TestClient(rest_app)

    ok = client.post("/refunds", params={"order_id": "ORD-004213", "amount": 42.0})
    assert ok.status_code == 200, ok.text
    assert ok.json()["refund_id"] == "RF-004213"

    bad = client.post("/refunds", params={"order_id": "o-99", "amount": 42.0})
    assert bad.status_code == 422, bad.text
    body = bad.json()
    assert body["detail"][0]["type"] == "string_pattern_mismatch"
    print("REST  422 body:", bad.text)


async def demo_mcp() -> None:
    ok = await call_issue_refund("ORD-004213", 42.0)
    assert not ok.is_error
    assert ok.structured_content["refund_id"] == "RF-004213"

    bad = await call_issue_refund("o-99", 42.0)
    assert bad.is_error, "a validation failure must arrive as isError, not an exception"
    remediation = bad.content[0].text
    assert "ORD-[0-9]{6}" in remediation
    assert "Retry" in remediation
    wire = bad.model_dump_json(by_alias=True)
    assert '"isError":true' in wire.replace(" ", "")
    print("MCP   isError wire:", wire)

    # The agent's next turn: it read the remediation, extracted the pattern,
    # and retried with a conforming argument. No code change, no redeploy.
    retry = await call_issue_refund("ORD-004213", 42.0)
    assert not retry.is_error
    assert retry.structured_content["order_id"] == "ORD-004213"
    print("MCP   retry succeeded:", retry.structured_content)


def main() -> None:
    demo_rest()
    asyncio.run(demo_mcp())
    print("OK — both behaviors asserted green.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Expected output (from the verified run):

REST  422 body: {"detail":[{"loc":["query","order_id"],"msg":"string does not match regex","type":"string_pattern_mismatch","input":"o-99"}]}
MCP   isError wire: {"_meta":null,"content":[{"type":"text","text":"order_id must match ORD-[0-9]{6}; you sent 'o-99'. Retry with a six-digit order id such as 'ORD-004213'.","annotations":null,"_meta":null}],"structuredContent":null,"isError":true,"resultType":"complete"}
MCP   retry succeeded: {'refund_id': 'RF-004213', 'order_id': 'ORD-004213', 'amount': 42.0}
OK — both behaviors asserted green.

Note the spelling split the demo makes visible: Python code reads result.is_error; the wire carries "isError": true. The SDK's pydantic models use snake_case in Python and camelCase on the wire, via aliases. When you read protocol docs or packet captures, expect the camelCase form.

1.x → 2.x rename note: tutorials written for MCP 1.x call the high-level builder FastMCP. In 2.x it is mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, and the client import is mcp.client.streamable_http.streamable_http_client (1.x: streamablehttp_client). The demo above uses the low-level mcp.server.lowlevel.Server deliberately, so you see the exact CallToolResult the protocol serializes. The MCPServer decorator API wraps the same handler machinery.

2.4 MCP wraps; it does not replace

Here is the temptation to refuse: agents are the new clients, so rewrite the API for agents. New endpoints, new shapes, new auth, designed agent-first from the domain down.

Count the cost before accepting it. You would throw away years of hardened invariants — the refund that either posts or does not, the authZ check that has survived three audits — and re-implement them in a layer where the caller is non-deterministic. You would put "probably correct" where determinism is load-bearing: money movement, permission decisions, durability. And you would ask every domain team to learn agent UX on top of their existing roadmap.

The cheaper architecture, and the one production MCP deployments converge on, is a wrapper: MCP as the Agentic Presentation Layer, the Backend-for-Agents. The deterministic core does not change. MCP servers sit atop it as adapters, translating business intents into domain API calls and translating domain results back into language an agent can act on.

The layering, top to bottom:

  • Hosts and agents. The reasoning loops. They hold user authentication and the model's API keys, and they decide.
  • MCP servers. Adapters. One per domain or bounded context, exposing coarse-grained intents with LLM-legible schemas and remediation text.
  • Deterministic core. Unchanged. REST, GraphQL, and gRPC services, Kafka topics and consumers, the databases behind them. Your topics do not change. Your gRPC services do not change. What changes is the surface through which a reasoning loop reaches them.

What stays in the microservice

Transactions and invariants. The refund either posts or it does not, and the tool does not get a vote. Authorization: who may refund whom, which the service has always decided. Idempotency keys, durability, exactly-once-ish delivery semantics, rate limits, quotas, and the schema truth for stored data.

These stay because they need determinism. A model must never own them. "Probably correct" is not a property money systems can have, and no remediation text can repair a double-posted refund. The microservice remains the system of record; the MCP layer is a system of access.

What moves to the MCP layer

Intent naming: verbs the model can choose between, at the granularity of turn economics. Schema shaping for LLM consumption: verbose, example-bearing, described in prose. Error remediation text: the self-healing contract from §2.3, which no REST service was ever asked to write. Progress and cancellation plumbing for long turns. Sampling: the server asking the host's model a question without ever holding its keys. Roots and subscriptions wiring: what context the agent may see, and how it learns when that context changes.

Notice the pattern. Everything that moved is about legibility to a reasoning loop. Everything that stayed is about correctness under adversity. The seam between them is the whole design.

The seam contract, and the anti-pattern

A tool is a deterministic function plus an LLM-legible wrapper. The body validates the arguments, calls the domain API, and translates the result — and the failures — into prose. It holds zero business invariants of its own beyond input shaping. If the refund rules change, they change in the billing service, and the tool picks them up without an edit.

The anti-pattern has a name: the smart proxy. A tool that re-implements the refund rules instead of calling the billing service. Two implementations of one rule is a fork. Forks drift. Drift becomes the 3 AM page when the tool's copy of the rule disagrees with the service's. If the logic matters, it lives behind the domain API. The tool is a translator, not a second brain.

That is the architectural shift in one paragraph. Contracts used to be written for compilers, and the deterministic core still is. MCP adds a layer written for readers: coarse intents, runtime discovery, prose errors that heal on the next turn — all of it a thin, honest adapter over systems that do not change. Wrap the core. Never fork it.

Module 3 — Converting Existing Microservice Domains to MCP for Agentic Use Cases

In plain language: Do not give a model every backend endpoint. Group work around user tasks, keep inputs and results small, and separate reading from actions that change data.

Most enterprises do not get to start with MCP. They start with a few hundred REST endpoints, built over a decade, owned by a dozen teams. Somewhere a ticket lands on your desk: "make the billing domain available to our agents." The tempting move is to run an OpenAPI-to-MCP generator and ship 200 tools by Friday. This module explains why that move fails, and what to do instead.

The core idea is simple. A REST API serves programs. An MCP server serves a reasoning model with a finite context window, fuzzy tool selection, and no patience for your database schema. Converting a domain means redesigning the affordance, not transliterating the endpoints. This module gives you four conversion patterns and a full refactoring blueprint, each with runnable code.

SDK note (1.x → 2.x): every example here uses mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer from MCP Python SDK 2.3.0. In SDK 1.x the same class was called FastMCP. The decorator names (@server.tool(), @server.resource()) are unchanged.

3.1 The 1:1 auto-generation anti-pattern

OpenAPI-to-MCP generators exist, and they work exactly as advertised: every endpoint becomes a tool, every schema becomes a parameter block. The output compiles. It also destroys agent performance in four measurable ways. Each one has a number attached, so you can argue it in a design review.

Token bloat eats the context window before reasoning starts. Every tool in the catalog costs tokens on every turn: the name, the description, the JSON Schema of its parameters, and often a response schema. A typical CRUD tool schema runs 300–600 tokens. Take the middle, 400. Multiply by 200 endpoints.

200 tools × 400 tokens ≈ 80,000 tokens of catalog, injected before the first reasoning token.

On a 200,000-token window, 40 percent of the model's working memory is now a phone book. The model has not read your question yet. It is already working with a handicap. Worse, most hosts re-send the tool list (or a large slice of it) on every turn, so the tax compounds across a multi-turn task.

Tool selection collapses under near-duplicates. A model picks tools the way a router picks ports: by matching the request against the catalog. With 200 fine-grained tools, the catalog is full of synonyms — getOrder, retrieveOrder, fetchOrderById, listOrders, searchOrders. The model's probability mass spreads across five plausible candidates instead of concentrating on one correct one. Precision and recall of tool choice fall off a cliff past a few dozen tools. Each wrong pick costs a wasted turn, an error recovery, and sometimes a side effect against the wrong entity. You did not give the agent 200 capabilities. You gave it 200 ways to hesitate.

One business workflow becomes 8–12 round-trips. Consider "refund this order." Against raw CRUD tools the agent must: fetch the order, fetch the payment, fetch the invoice, check the refund policy, post the refund, update the order status, and confirm. That is 4 semantic steps expressed as 8–12 tool calls once you count pagination, retries, and correlating IDs between calls. Every call is a model turn plus a network round-trip — typically 1–3 seconds each. Ten calls means 20–30 seconds of latency and ten independent chances to fail, time out, or lose the thread. The workflow knew what it wanted. The tooling made it spell it out one syllable at a time.

Internal database shape leaks into the model's world. Auto-generated tools return whatever the endpoint returns: foreign-key UUIDs, audit columns (created_by, row_version, deleted_at), soft-delete flags, internal risk scores. Three bad things follow. First, tokens burn on columns the agent can never act on. Second, the agent starts inventing joins — "find orders where customer_id equals…" — using hallucinated UUIDs, because the catalog taught it that UUIDs are how you navigate. Third, and most dangerous, writable internal fields become writable by the model. An agent that can set created_by to itself or flip deleted_at is a data-integrity incident waiting for a Tuesday.

The rule that replaces the generator: tools are an agent affordance, not an API mirror. Design them for the model's needs — coarse intents, pruned payloads, safe defaults — and the four costs above shrink by an order of magnitude. The next four sections are the patterns that do it.

3.2 The four conversion patterns — overview

The diagram below maps the territory. Each pattern attacks one of the four costs from §3.1. You will usually apply all four to the same domain, in this order: aggregate intents first, prune payloads second, split reads from writes third, and guard large payloads last.

3.3 Pattern 1 — Intent-Driven Aggregation (workflow facade)

Why. An agent thinks in business intents: "can this order ship?", "refund the damaged item", "where is my invoice?". Your microservices think in entities: users, orders, stock rows. Every gap between those two vocabularies is paid for in tool calls. The 1:1 mapping forces the agent to do the joining — fetch the order, read the warehouse_id, fetch the stock, fetch the user — which is exactly the 8–12 round-trip problem from §3.1. The fix is a facade: one coarse-grained tool per business intent that fans out to the fine-grained services concurrently and returns a single composed answer.

The facade also hides join keys. The agent never learns that orders carry a warehouse_id foreign key, so it can never hallucinate a join across one. The join happens in Python, where it belongs.

The mechanics. The tool resolves the entity graph itself, uses asyncio.gather() for the independent downstream calls, and composes the result into prose or compact markdown — the shapes models reason over best. Downstream services stay untouched. Only the MCP layer changes.

Runnable example. Three mocked services, one intent tool. The mock uses httpx.MockTransport, so this runs with no network. Copy it into a file and run it — it prints the composed decision and asserts the fan-out happened.

"""Pattern 1: Intent-Driven Aggregation. One coarse-grained intent tool fans out
to three microservices concurrently with asyncio.gather(), then composes a
single agent-sized answer. Downstream services are mocked with
httpx.MockTransport (no network)."""
import asyncio
import httpx
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer

# --- Mock downstream microservices -------------------------------------------
USERS = {"u-101": {"id": "u-101", "name": "Awanish Singh", "tier": "gold",
                   "email": "a.singh@example.com"}}
ORDERS = {"o-9001": {"id": "o-9001", "user_id": "u-101", "total": 248.50,
                     "items": [{"sku": "KB-01", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "MS-07", "qty": 1}],
                     "warehouse_id": "w-east-2", "status": "packed"}}
STOCK = {("w-east-2", "KB-01"): 140, ("w-east-2", "MS-07"): 12}

def mock_handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    path = request.url.path
    if path.startswith("/users/"):
        user = USERS.get(path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
        return httpx.Response(200, json=user) if user else httpx.Response(404)
    if path.startswith("/orders/"):
        order = ORDERS.get(path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
        return httpx.Response(200, json=order) if order else httpx.Response(404)
    if path.startswith("/stock/"):
        wid, sku = path.rsplit("/", 2)[-2:]
        return httpx.Response(200, json={"warehouse_id": wid, "sku": sku,
                                         "on_hand": STOCK.get((wid, sku), 0)})
    return httpx.Response(404, json={"error": "unknown route"})

transport = httpx.MockTransport(mock_handler)

async def get_user(client: httpx.AsyncClient, user_id: str) -> dict:
    r = await client.get(f"http://user-svc/users/{user_id}")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

async def get_order(client: httpx.AsyncClient, order_id: str) -> dict:
    r = await client.get(f"http://order-svc/orders/{order_id}")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

async def get_stock(client: httpx.AsyncClient, warehouse_id: str, sku: str) -> dict:
    r = await client.get(f"http://warehouse-svc/stock/{warehouse_id}/{sku}")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

# --- MCP server: ONE intent tool replaces three fine-grained calls ------------
server = MCPServer("fulfillment-mcp", version="1.0.0")

@server.tool()
async def fulfill_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Answer 'can this order ship right now?' in one call.

    Fans out to User, Order and Warehouse services concurrently, then composes
    a single shipment decision. The agent never sees three services or their
    join keys — it sees one business intent.
    """
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport) as client:
        # The order is fetched first: it names the user and the warehouse,
        # which the other two calls depend on.
        order = await get_order(client, order_id)
        user, *stocks = await asyncio.gather(
            get_user(client, order["user_id"]),
            *[get_stock(client, order["warehouse_id"], item["sku"])
              for item in order["items"]],
        )
    short = [(s["sku"], item["qty"], s["on_hand"])
             for s, item in zip(stocks, order["items"])
             if s["on_hand"] < item["qty"]]
    lines = [f"# Shipment decision — order {order_id}", "",
             f"- Customer: {user['name']} (tier: {user['tier']})",
             f"- Order total: ${order['total']:.2f} · status: {order['status']}", ""]
    if short:
        lines.append("- CANNOT SHIP — short stock: " + ", ".join(
            f"{sku} (need {need}, have {have})" for sku, need, have in short))
    else:
        lines.append("- READY TO SHIP — all line items in stock at "
                     + order["warehouse_id"])
    return "\n".join(lines)

async def main() -> None:
    result = await server.call_tool("fulfill_order", {"order_id": "o-9001"})
    text = result.content[0].text
    print(text)
    assert "Awanish Singh" in text and "READY TO SHIP" in text
    print("\nOne tool call replaced 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 downstream round-trips.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Output:

# Shipment decision — order o-9001

- Customer: Awanish Singh (tier: gold)
- Order total: $248.50 · status: packed

- READY TO SHIP — all line items in stock at w-east-2

One tool call replaced 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 downstream round-trips.

Three things to carry into production. First, the fan-out needs a timeout budget: wrap the gather in asyncio.wait_for so one slow service cannot hold the agent's turn hostage. Second, decide the partial-failure policy up front — if the warehouse call fails but the order call succeeded, do you return a degraded answer ("order packed, stock unknown") or fail the whole tool? Degraded answers beat exceptions for agents; an isError result (which the server returns as a normal CallToolResult, per the wire facts in the Writer Guide) lets the model self-heal. Third, keep the facade stateless. The moment the tool starts remembering things between calls, you have built a shadow database. Composition is fine. Caching entity state inside the tool is a consistency bug with a friendly face.

3.4 Pattern 2 — Context Pruning & Schema Flattening

Why. Every byte of a tool result is rented context-window space. Service payloads were designed for programs: they carry audit columns, UUID join keys, currency in minor units, and nesting five levels deep because some other service might need it. The model needs none of that. It needs the order number, the total, the items, and the status — in that order, in flat prose. Pruning is not cosmetic. In the example below, one realistic order payload costs 294 tokens raw and 24 tokens pruned. At 200 orders a day of agentic traffic, that is the difference between a session that stays coherent and one that starts dropping earlier turns to make room for row_version.

Pruning also closes the leakage hole from §3.1. A field the agent never receives cannot be hallucinated into a filter, and cannot be written back. The MCP layer is the right place for this because it owns the agent-facing contract — the services keep their internal shape, and every agent gets the same pruned view.

The mechanics. Define the agent-facing shape as a Pydantic model with only the fields the model may reason about. Map once, in one function, at the MCP boundary. Prefer flat markdown or a flat model over nested JSON. Models parse prose more reliably than they traverse trees. Flat shapes also survive truncation: a cut-off nested object is garbage, while a cut-off bullet list is still half the facts.

Runnable example. A raw order payload with audit columns, UUID keys, and nested fulfillment internals goes in; a flat summary comes out. The script computes the token delta itself with the rough len(text) // 4 heuristic used throughout this module.

"""Pattern 2: Context Pruning & Schema Flattening. The MCP layer strips audit
columns, UUID join keys and deep nesting into a flat, LLM-sized shape, and
reports the token delta."""
import asyncio
import json
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer

def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Rough token estimate used across this module: ~4 chars per token."""
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)

# --- What the microservice actually returns (raw, internal shape) -------------
RAW_ORDER = {
    "order_id": "9f3c2a1e-7b4d-4c8f-9e2a-1d5f6c7b8a90",
